result:
I've written and queued the fix for #424, but nothing is measured on a device yet: ten Thor soaks are waiting in the dispatcher queue. PR #434 stays a draft until they are judged. I posted `[lane.tbchurn424] waiting:` on #434 and #424, so `handback.sh` resumes the lane when the results land.

**What the churn costs on master.** On Crimson Skies' flying route (`crimson-skies`), the jump-cache wipes and the dirty re-arm walks take **23.9% of the emulated CPU thread**, at a median of 23 fps. The build's own counters time this directly (read from soak `titleplay-p1-crimson`, Thor). That figure is a bound: what the two mechanisms cost now, not what removing them will give back. In every window, none of the discarded code blocks had a byte written: the guest writes data that happens to share a page with code. Hands-off Crimson churns only 0.2–1.4%. lane.tcgchurn measured it that way, which is why it concluded the problem wasn't there.

**The change** (`cb66484748`, in `accel/tcg/tb-maint.c` and `cputlb.c`):
- **Range test restored.** This is upstream QEMU's behaviour: a write throws away only the blocks whose own bytes it touched. It carries the guards from the held `937848c9e7`: already-dead blocks and superblocks are always discarded.
- **Per-page code bitmap.** A write that touches no translated byte is answered under one page lock, with no list walk and no per-write allocation. The bitmap only ever over-covers the code on a page. A leftover bit costs one extra walk; it cannot let a rewritten block keep running.
- **Kill switch.** `HAKUX_TCG424_WHOLEPAGE=1` restores the old whole-page behaviour at runtime.
- **New counters.** The per-2-second `[tlb68]` log line gains `rt=`, `cb=` and `cbb=`.
- **Checks so far.** Both files compile clean with the desktop build's flags; the only warning is one already in master's code. Preflight passes. It has not been built for Android locally; the dispatcher builds each ref.

**The A/B.** A is master (`7e6a4ac88a`), B is my branch (`1d1251aa4b`), same Thor, runs interleaved. Crimson on the flying route gets 3 runs per arm. Blinx gets 2 per arm as the cost-side title: it only churns 2%, but takes 50k slow writes a second, so it is where keeping more code pages write-trapped could hurt. The pass/fail conditions are registered in `tbchurn424-soak.json` and read with `docs/lanes/tbchurn424/churn.py`:
- **The counter that must move:** the churn share of the CPU thread must fall to 5% or below on B. If it doesn't, the fix is inert here, and I'll report that rather than tune.
- **The cost:** slow writes are reported, and the bitmap must answer at least 80% of them.
- **The fps that counts:** Crimson must gain at least 2 fps.
- **No regression:** Blinx must not drop more than 1 fps.

The pgraph "no suite regresses" check (`tbchurn424-pixels-inert.json`, 8 suites, captures must be identical) was committed with its refs; that commit is what queues it for the arms job.

**Risk:** the fix makes invalidation do less, so if it's wrong, a game that rewrites its own code runs stale code. The pgraph suites barely exercise that. So the evidence will be the two titles playing normally, plus the kill switch as a fallback.

The request ids and all of the above are in `docs/lanes/tbchurn424/NOTES.md`. The Claude Docs connector (Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive too) needs authorising in claude.ai's connector settings before this session can use it; nothing here needed it.
